from-ymd-opt.title: How NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt() works
from-ymd-opt.description: Builds a date from year, month and day; impossible dates give None.

note.text: Option: Some(date) or None for a date that does not exist

slides.caption: from_ymd_opt() checks that the month is 1 to 12 and that the day exists in that month of that year.
Leap years: divisible by 4, except century years, which must be divisible by 400 (2000 was a leap year, 1900 was not). 2024 is a leap year.
Day 29 exists: the result is Some(2024-02-29).
Day 30 does not exist in February, so the result is None instead of a panic or a silently corrected date.
Use from_ymd_opt() with user input and handle None. from_ymd() (no _opt) panics on bad dates and is deprecated.

parse-from-str.title: How NaiveDate::parse_from_str() works
parse-from-str.description: Reads a date from text using a format string.

slides.caption: parse_from_str() walks the text and the format side by side. %-codes read a field; other characters must appear exactly.
The / in the format must match a / in the text. It does.
Another /, then %Y reads the year: 2024. The date is checked like from_ymd_opt().
The result is Ok(2024-03-15). Text that does not fit the format, like "2024-03-15", gives Err(ParseError).

format.title: How NaiveDate::format() works
format.description: Writes a date as text using a format string.

slides.caption: format() replaces every %-code with part of the date. Other characters, here the spaces, are copied as they are.
%A is the full weekday name: 2024-03-15 is a Friday.
%d is the day of the month with 2 digits: 15.
%B is the full month name: March.
format() returns a DelayedFormat; to_string() (or {} in format!) produces "Friday 15 March 2024". Names are in English.

checked-add-days.title: How NaiveDate::checked_add_days() works
checked-add-days.description: Adds a number of days and moves into the next month when needed.

slides.caption: checked_add_days() counts forward one calendar day at a time. January has 31 days.
+1: January 31, the last day of January.
+2: there is no January 32, so the month changes: February 1.
The result is Some(2024-02-02). It is None only if the date would leave chrono's range (about ±262,000 years).

checked-sub-days.title: How NaiveDate::checked_sub_days() works
checked-sub-days.description: Subtracts days and moves into the previous month when needed.

slides.caption: checked_sub_days() counts back. The day before the 1st of a month is the last day of the previous month.
One day back leaves March. February 2024 has 29 days (leap year), so the day before is February 29.
In 2023, not a leap year, the same step would give February 28.
The result is Some(2024-02-29). The calendar decides; you never have to know how long a month is.

checked-add-months.title: How NaiveDate::checked_add_months() works
checked-add-months.description: Adds months; a day that does not exist is clamped to the end of the month.

slides.caption: checked_add_months() changes the month number and keeps the day, if that day exists.
January + 1 month is February. The day would stay 31.
chrono clamps the day to the last day of the month instead of rolling over into March.
Clamping means the steps do not add up: 2024-01-31 + 1 month + 1 month is 2024-03-29, but + 2 months is 2024-03-31.
The result is Some(2024-02-29). Use checked_add_days() when you need an exact number of days instead.

signed-duration-since.title: How NaiveDate::signed_duration_since() works
signed-duration-since.description: The time between two dates, as a TimeDelta.

slides.caption: signed_duration_since() subtracts the argument from self and returns a TimeDelta (called Duration in older versions).
From February 1 to March 1 is exactly the length of February.
February 2024 has 29 days, so the difference is 29 days. num_days() reads that as a number.
"Signed" means the order matters: the other way round gives −29 days.
mar1 − feb1 = 29 days. The - operator does the same: (mar1 - feb1).num_days() is 29.

weekday.title: How Datelike::weekday() works
weekday.description: Gives the day of the week of a date.

slides.caption: weekday() comes from the Datelike trait (use chrono::Datelike). It returns a Weekday value.
chrono stores enough about each year to know which weekday its days fall on, so no counting from a fixed date is needed.
Weekday has helpers: number_from_monday() is 5, num_days_from_sunday() is 5, succ() is Sat.
date.weekday() is Weekday::Fri; it prints as "Fri". Weeks start on Monday in chrono.

ordinal.title: How Datelike::ordinal() works
ordinal.description: The day of the year, from 1 to 365 (or 366).

slides.caption: ordinal() counts the days from January 1 (day 1) up to the date.
All of January comes before the date: 31 days.
All of February: 29 days, because 2024 is a leap year.
Added up: 61. In 2023 the same date would be day 60.
ordinal() is 61 (1-based); ordinal0() is 60. Datelike is the trait; NaiveDate implements it.

iso-week.title: How Datelike::iso_week() works
iso-week.description: The ISO 8601 week number; a date can belong to a week of the next year.

slides.caption: ISO weeks run Monday to Sunday. Week 1 of a year is the week that holds that year's first Thursday.
The week that starts on Monday 30 December 2024 runs until Sunday 5 January 2025.
Its Thursday is 2 January 2025, so this whole week is week 1 of 2025.
So 30 December 2024 is in week 1 of 2025, even though its calendar year is 2024.
iso_week() returns an IsoWeek; .week() is 1 and .year() is 2025. Use .year() from the IsoWeek, not date.year(), for week-based reports.
succ_opt() gives the following day ("successor"). pred_opt() gives the day before.
2024 is a leap year, so February has a 29th day: that is the next day.
In 2023, the next day after February 28 would be March 1.
succ_opt() is Some(2024-02-29). It is None only at the very last date chrono can represent.

iter-days.title: How NaiveDate::iter_days() works
iter-days.description: An endless iterator over the following days, starting with the date itself.

slides.caption: iter_days() yields the date, then the day after, and so on, forever. take(4) stops after 4 dates.
The first item is the start date itself.
Then February 29: the iterator knows 2024 is a leap year.
Then March 1. take(4) has its 4 items, so iteration stops.
Without take() the loop would only stop at the end of chrono's range. iter_weeks() steps by 7 days.

time-from-hms-opt.title: How NaiveTime::from_hms_opt() works
time-from-hms-opt.description: Builds a time of day; impossible times give None.

slides.caption: from_hms_opt() checks each part of the time before building it.
So the result is Some(14:30:00), half past two in the afternoon.
A day has hours 0 to 23. 25 is out of range.
The result is None. It does not wrap around to 01:00 of the next day.
NaiveTime has no date and no time zone. Combine it with a date using date.and_time(t) or and_hms_opt().

and-hms-opt.title: How NaiveDate::and_hms_opt() works
and-hms-opt.description: Combines a date with a time of day into a NaiveDateTime.

slides.caption: and_hms_opt() checks the time like NaiveTime::from_hms_opt() and attaches it to the date.
Together they make a NaiveDateTime: a date and a time, still without a time zone.
The result is Some(2024-03-15 14:30:00). To fix it to a time zone, use .and_utc() or a TimeZone such as Local.

with-ymd-and-hms.title: How TimeZone::with_ymd_and_hms works
with-ymd-and-hms.description: Builds a DateTime in a time zone from its parts.

slides.caption: In zones with daylight saving a local time can be missing or happen twice, so the answer is wrapped.
Read the parts in the zone.
UTC has no gaps: exactly one answer.
Call .unwrap() or .single() to get the DateTime.
The same instant has the same timestamp in every zone.

slides.caption: The offset in the text is kept. Convert with with_timezone(&Utc) to compare instants.
Date, time and offset are read.
The same instant in UTC is 10:30.
Errors on text that is not RFC 3339.
The weekday must match the date.
